name: Hana Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43, with a bachelor’s degree, and I maintain library-loan software for a tech company. I know the code well enough to handle ordinary faults, though I still take tricky cases to another developer. Jules drives a school bus, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage; I like clearing a wrongly charged fee before a family has to argue about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team that the library-loan app still needs someone who knows why a borrowed book appears missing. I use AI sometimes to draft a check, then compare it with a real loan record before release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a bachelor’s degree and a mid-level developer job at ordinary pay, with about four months of basic expenses saved. My partner Jules drives a school bus; with two children and a mortgage, our bills are covered while both wages keep coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep fixing loan-account errors and ask the library desk for three disputed returns each month. We would continue saving 180 monthly if both wages hold and put off replacing the dining table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about this picture. The mortgage is there, but a small AI change does not make my pay look shaky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when a book is marked missing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A child returned a book that the scanner failed to register, and a fee went to the family. I traced the scan time against the desk receipt before the fee was removed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep four months saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bus route stops during some school breaks, and Jules has other shifts but not the same pay every month. Four months lets us handle that without asking our parents for groceries.

I compare occasional **AI checks** with desk receipts before release.
think: I have **four months saved** and ordinary mid-level pay.
I expect both wages to cover our **mortgage and children** while work stays steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our staff association that AI taking checking, booking and coding will reach the library platform. I would ask for written staffing numbers and paid time to learn before anybody’s hours are changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The easy loan fixes could be done by software, while I am left checking many more exceptions. My hours might shrink if the company decides one developer can cover several libraries, and Jules’s bus shifts cannot carry the mortgage alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d ask a colleague to show me an AI way to find a duplicate return, then test it against old cases on our safe system if my manager approves paid practice time. In the first year I’d join the staff association’s meeting on staffing and ask what happens to the library support team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my own hours and irritated by vague reassurances. I want to see what the tool actually catches before telling anyone it will help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the association to demand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A count of developer and support posts, and a rule about who checks a disputed fee. I would not accept a slide saying everyone can be retrained without time on the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you judge the AI test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feed it the scanner error that charged the child and five other old returns. If it misses the child’s receipt, it has not earned a release.

fieldNote: She demands **paid practice time** and a specific six-case test before trusting AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write and check most of my library software, and workers need a written account of what happens to jobs. Robots for hands-on bus driving may arrive around 2031, so Jules’s work has a later date than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my developer role could end before we build more savings, and other local firms may be using the same AI. Four months would cover bills briefly, but not two children and a mortgage for a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the staff association now to seek written notice and paid transition terms. If full AGI arrives in 2028 and I am cut, I’d apply for paid library customer-service openings only if posts exist and wages cover our bills; Jules and I would cancel the planned patio work to keep cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed, though I can still list steps. My worry is seeing the mortgage leave the account while my old badge stops opening the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell the children about the patio?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the yard can wait because the house payment comes first. They can still play outside; they do not need to carry my job fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would library service last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know. AI can answer borrowers too, so I would treat a paid offer as a bridge and keep looking at what work is actually open.

I know **bus robots around 2031** come later than my screen-work shock.
think: I expect **my developer role** could end even with several nearby firms.
I know **four months saved** cannot support a long search and mortgage.

fieldNote: She links the **2028 thinking date** to software, with Jules’s bus exposure following later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years before full AGI in 2031 gives us time to test what a library worker still has to decide about a disputed fee. Robots for bus routes may follow around 2034, but the code reaches its date first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn more about borrower complaints while I am paid, though AI may eventually do that reasoning too. Jules and I could build a larger cushion if both incomes continue, but the school-break pattern limits what we can save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the library support lead for one paid half-day each quarter listening to disputes, and attend only if my company and the lead approve it. Separately, we’d save 130 monthly if both incomes arrive; after 2031 I’d seek paid borrower-support jobs only if my developer role ends and vacancies cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious but able to prepare. I would not call a proposed visit experience until someone gives me the time to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn from a dispute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d hear whether the borrower has a desk receipt, a return slot photo or nothing written down. The answer changes how the fee should be checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the support lead has no time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for anonymized old cases to review during my normal paid work, if my manager agrees. I would keep coding rather than quietly take unpaid leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade before full AGI in 2036 gives libraries time to settle rules for borrower fees and train workers properly. Robots for hands-on bus driving may come around 2039, after software changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children would be older by then, but the mortgage may still need both wages. I could build six months of basic bills and learn the policy side of library service, without assuming that work is safe from AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep maintaining loan accounts and study one anonymized disputed-fee case monthly with the support lead if my manager approves paid time. Separately, Jules and I would save 160 monthly when both incomes arrive; if my developer role ends after 2036, I’d apply for paid library-policy support only where vacancies remain and pay covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy about the far job change but steady about the next few years. I want rules people can understand, not a stack of automated fees nobody will explain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What rule would you start with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d write a plain appeal path for a borrower who has a return receipt. If an AI system flags a fee, a named worker should still review the evidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave this town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a written paid offer that covers the new housing cost and the children’s school travel. There are some developer jobs nearby, so I would test those first if I needed work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because library code could be automated before I find a paid path elsewhere. Written notice, paid transition time and a real library-service offer that covers our mortgage would help; I would not ask our children to carry the worry.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who explains a fee after a computer decides it. I would want a named worker and a plain appeal route, even when the first check is automated. A library fee needs a named worker and a plain appeal route, even when AI checks it first.

headlineQuote: A library fee needs a named worker and a plain appeal route, even when AI checks it first.
portrait: Hana is a **43-year-old mid-level developer** with a bachelor’s degree, ordinary pay and four months of expenses saved.
She and Jules cover **two children** and a mortgage, though school-break bus pay varies.
She uses AI **occasionally** and tests it against library receipts before trusting it.
She asks the **staff association** for paid learning and written job terms.
The **2028 scenario** threatens her coding wage before bus-driving robots arrive later.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her library software wage before a viable paid move.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, paid transition time and a bill-covering library-service offer would help.
